lead: Modular arithmetic is arithmetic on a clock. You count as usual, but after a fixed number n you wrap back to 0. Two integers that land on the same tick are congruent. This single idea powers RSA, Diffie–Hellman and SHA, and it lets a computer handle 2048-bit numbers while storing only 2048 bits per value. It is the arithmetic behind every public-key system in these notes.
prereq: You need school arithmetic: remainders, multiplication and powers; Unit 1's security goals give context only.

blocks.text: Fix a positive integer n, called the modulus, with n ≥ 2. Two integers a and b are congruent modulo n when n divides a − b. We write a ≡ b (mod n). Here n divides a − b means (a − b)/n is an integer.
That is the same as saying a and b leave the same remainder when divided by n. For example, 17 ≡ 5 (mod 12), because 17 − 5 = 12.

Every integer belongs to one residue class modulo n: the set of all integers with the same remainder. The class is named by its least non-negative remainder. Modulo 5, the class of 2 is {..., −8, −3, 2, 7, 12, ...}. The set of all classes is Z<sub>n</sub> = {0, 1, ..., n−1}.

A negative number is reduced by adding n until it lies in 0 to n−1: −3 ≡ 2 (mod 5). Congruence is an equivalence relation: every integer is congruent to itself, the order of a and b does not matter, and if a ≡ b and b ≡ c then a ≡ c.
Addition, subtraction and multiplication follow one rule: do the ordinary operation, then take the remainder modulo n. The answer is always in Z<sub>n</sub>.
(a + b) mod n = ((a mod n) + (b mod n)) mod n
blocks.where: a and b are integers; n is the modulus, a positive integer with n ≥ 2; mod returns the least non-negative remainder.

blocks.text: Modulo 7: 5 + 6 = 11 ≡ 4; 5 × 6 = 30 ≡ 2; 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 4. For subtraction, 3 − 5 = −2 ≡ 5 (mod 7). Modulo 12, 9 + 8 = 17 ≡ 5, and 9 × 8 = 72 ≡ 0. The clock face uses n = 12: 10 + 4 = 2, since 14:00 is 2 PM.
Multiplication is always possible. Division is not: 3 ÷ 5 modulo 7 means multiplying by the inverse of 5, which Section 4 covers. Powers are repeated multiplication, so they reduce the same way.

Naive exponentiation computes a^e by e − 1 multiplications. If e has 300 digits, that is more operations than there are atoms in the observable universe. Square-and-multiply uses the binary digits of e instead.

items: Write the exponent e in binary.
Read the bits from left to right. Square R. If the bit is 1, multiply R by a. Reduce modulo n after every squaring and multiplication.
Equivalently, build a¹, a², a⁴, a⁸, ... by squaring, then multiply the entries whose bit is 1.

blocks.text: Cost: about log₂ e squarings and at most log₂ e multiplications, so O(log e) modular multiplications. For 7²³, the binary exponent is 10111. Five squarings and three extra multiplications replace 22 multiplications.
Never reduce the exponent modulo n. Exponent reduction uses φ(n) and is covered in Chapter 2.5. The figure traces the method for 7²³ mod 13.
An inverse of a modulo n is an integer b with a·b ≡ 1 (mod n). We write b = a⁻¹ mod n. It exists if and only if gcd(a, n) = 1. Then it is unique in Z<sub>n</sub>.

Why: if d = gcd(a, n) > 1, every multiple a·b is divisible by d, so a·b − 1 is not, and cannot be a multiple of n. If gcd(a, n) = 1, the extended Euclidean algorithm gives integers x and y with a·x + n·y = 1, so a·x ≡ 1 (mod n).
Examples: 3⁻¹ ≡ 5 (mod 7) because 15 ≡ 1. 5⁻¹ ≡ 7 (mod 17) because 5 × 7 = 35 = 2 × 17 + 1. 6 has no inverse modulo 9 because gcd(6, 9) = 3.

To divide by a modulo n, multiply by a⁻¹. This is legal only when gcd(a, n) = 1. When n is prime, every a from 1 to n−1 has gcd(a, n) = 1, so every non-zero element is invertible; Zp is a field (see Chapter 2.3).

spec.aria: Five cells for 7 to the powers 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 mod 13, each with the bit of 23 below it; four have bit 1 and are multiplied in three steps to give 2.

examples.question: Compute 7²³ mod 13 using square-and-multiply. Show the powers and the final multiplication.
steps: Write 23 in binary: 23 = 16 + 4 + 2 + 1, so the bits for 2⁴, 2³, 2², 2¹, 2⁰ are 1, 0, 1, 1, 1.
The bits equal to 1 are 16, 4, 2 and 1, so 7²³ ≡ 7¹⁶ × 7⁴ × 7² × 7¹ ≡ 9 × 9 × 10 × 7 (mod 13).
examples.check:
print(pow(7, 1, 13))
print(pow(7, 2, 13))
print(pow(7, 4, 13))
print(pow(7, 8, 13))
print(pow(7, 16, 13))
print(pow(7, 23, 13))

traps: a ≡ b (mod n) is not ordinary equality. It says n divides a − b. For example, 17 ≡ 5 (mod 12) but 17 ≠ 5.
Reducing an exponent modulo n. In 7²³ mod 13, 23 mod 13 = 10 and 7¹⁰ ≡ 4, not 2. Exponent reduction uses φ(n) and needs gcd(base, n) = 1 (Chapter 2.5).
Assuming every number has an inverse. 2 has no inverse modulo 4 because gcd(2, 4) = 2; an inverse exists only when gcd(a, n) = 1.
Leaving a negative answer. −3 mod 5 is 2, not −3; add n until the result is in 0 to n−1.

quiz.a: a ≡ b (mod n) when n divides a − b, that is, a and b leave the same remainder on division by n.

quiz.q: State the condition for a to have an inverse modulo n.
quiz.a: gcd(a, n) = 1; the inverse is then unique in Z_n.

quiz.q: Explain why 2 has no inverse modulo 4.
quiz.a: Any product 2b is even, so 2b − 1 is odd and cannot be a multiple of 4. Equivalently gcd(2, 4) = 2 ≠ 1.

quiz.q: Why does square-and-multiply take O(log e) multiplications rather than O(e)?
quiz.a: It uses the binary digits of e. Each bit needs one squaring, plus one multiplication when the bit is 1. There are about log₂ e bits, so about 2 log₂ e modular multiplications.

quiz.q: A student computes 3²⁰ mod 7 as 3^(20 mod 7) = 3⁶ ≡ 1. Is the method valid? Give the correct value.
quiz.a: No. Reducing the exponent modulo the modulus is not valid. Since gcd(3, 7) = 1, reduce the exponent modulo φ(7) = 6: 20 ≡ 2 (mod 6), so 3²⁰ ≡ 3² = 9 ≡ 2 (mod 7).

beyond: Not for the exam. Real cryptographic libraries never use the schoolbook method above. They use Montgomery multiplication, which replaces division by n with shifts and additions, and Barrett reduction for large batches. Implementations must also run in constant time so that timing leaks do not reveal secret exponents, a real side-channel attack. Search for “Montgomery modular multiplication” and “constant-time modular exponentiation” to go deeper.
